abstract: Sex allocation, the division of resources between male and female function, often varies as a function of size in cosexual plants. This variation is thought to evolve because fitness returns gained from allocating to each function are influenced by plant size, and many mechanisms have been proposed for why it should be so. Here, we explore how competing selfing and limited seed dispersal jointly shape the evolution of size-dependent sex allocation in an annual plant population where size is environmentally determined. First assuming that the quality of habitat patches changes every generation, we show that competing selfing favours increased femaleness with size, whereas limited seed dispersal selects in the opposite direction. Which of the two mechanisms prevails depends on the selfing and seed dispersal rates, as well as on the severity inbreeding depression. Then, we let patch-quality differences persist over several generations and show that such persistence generates an additional selective pressure on sex allocation when seed dispersal is limited. Environmental persistence favours larger plants to allocate more resource to female function, as producing more seeds increases the probability that their own offspring settle on their high-quality patch in the next generation.
